captions.text: Recap of chapter 18: an eval is fixed cases with automatic checks.
You run each case several times, because one run tells you little.
A difference only counts if it's bigger than an agent against itself.
And the failures tell you more than the score. Today, Part 4 begins.
Today's black box: searching by meaning.
Let's open it.
Quillon Coffee, an invented chain, has a handbook of 42 files. Which holds the answer?
Start with word search. Each file scores one point for each question word it holds.
Predict: two questions. The first uses the handbook's words. The second doesn't.
The till float is right. The footwear question is wrong, and nothing says so.
The answer is in uniform.md, under "shoe allowance". It never says "footwear".
An embedding model doesn't reply. It turns text into a list of numbers: a vector.
Predict: will 20 repeated sentences give a longer list than one word?
No. Both are 768 numbers, so any two texts can be compared.
Similar meanings get similar numbers. That's what the model was trained to do.
To compare vectors, think of them as arrows. Cosine asks: same direction?
The dot product multiplies them number by number, and adds it all up.
Dividing by both lengths removes length, so only direction counts.
Vectors small enough to check by hand. Predict: what will [3, 4] and [6, 8] score?
1, because they point the same way. Length doesn't count.
At right angles gives 0. Opposite gives -1.
Now real text. The footwear question, against three handbook sentences.
Predict: the first sentence shares no useful word. Which will score highest?
The shoe allowance wins, and nobody gave the model a list of synonyms.
But the roastery still scores 0.476. A score isn't a percentage.
A vector store keeps vectors, and finds the closest. This one is a plain list.
That's all of vector search: score every row, sort, keep the top k.
Index joins an embedder to a store, so your code works in plain text.
Documents get embedded once. Each question gets embedded when you ask it.
One chunk for each whole file, then the same two questions.
Predict: will the footwear question find uniform.md this time?
Yes, in first place. Word search put expenses.md first.
Two questions prove nothing. Here are 22, fixed before we measured.
Each search gets a point for a right file first, and in its top 3.
Predict: will vectors win all three groups?
Direct questions: a draw, 8 of 8 each.
Reworded: vectors got 4 first, words got 2. Both of those were ties.
Codes: vectors didn't win. And they still missed half the reworded questions.
Rebuilt five times, every top 3 matched. The limit here is 22 questions.
Now four questions the handbook can't answer.
Predict: will their scores be clearly lower?
No. Search always returns something, and dogs scored 0.720.
The script also checks the 16 right answers. 7 scored below that, so no cut-off works.
A score says how close the topic is. It doesn't say the answer is there.
Chroma is a real vector database. Same add, same search.
Importing it here means whitebox works without it. Chroma needs Python 3.12 to 3.14.
Chroma reports distance, so 1 minus distance gives our score back.
Index didn't change. Only the store did.
Same scores as the list store. All 22 questions gave the same top 5.
Run it again, and no documents get embedded. The rows are on disk.
A database remembers. Predict: what if you add the same chunks twice?
84 rows, and no error. uniform.md fills two of your three results.
So check the count before you add.
Your turn. Open exercises.py and complete the five TODOs.
You'll build your own store behind the same methods. No Ollama needed.
You've finished when you see 5 passed.
